talks.summary:
Overview: Nathan Nye (True Anomaly) and Philip Toan (Ledger) present at Hardwear.io on exploiting keyspace reduction and relay attacks against 3DES and AES-protected NFC tags.

Key Topics: NFC authentication weaknesses in access control; relay attacks over sub-gigahertz links; keyspace reduction techniques; prior MIFARE Classic vulnerability research; and live card unlocking demonstration.

Technical Details: Researchers demonstrate authenticating with a locked NFC card via relay, then updating configuration to unlock memory pages from 10 of 48 to 44 of 48 accessible. The attack chains relay communication with an unlock-mode configuration write.

Takeaways: AES and 3DES-protected NFC implementations remain vulnerable to relay attacks. Physical access control deployments should not assume cryptographic protection alone prevents cloning.

talks.title: The IoT Longevity Crisis: Managing Obsolete Security and "Cloud Slop" with Yossi Oren
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The IoT Longevity Crisis: Managing Obsolete Security and "Cloud Slop" with Yossi Oren.
talks.summary:
IoT Longevity Problem

Yossi Oren discusses how IoT product lifecycles diverge from vendor lifecycles. Devices may remain deployed for decades after companies, engineers, and smart features fade—illustrated by a fridge stuck in 2017. Sensors and actuators outlast the software and hardware supporting them.

Critical Infrastructure Exposure

Unlike home devices behind a perimeter, field-deployed IoT on bridges, traffic lights, and dams is physically accessible. Compromised devices can become network stepping stones, and upgrades on critical systems like dams carry operational risk when original designers are gone.

Separating Actuation from Cloud Slop

Oren advocates decoupling durable actuation from ephemeral "AI cloud slop" smart features so core functions survive when cloud services end. Sustainability demands planning for decades-long device lifetimes.

Documentation and AI

He urges writing imperfect documentation and teardown videos that future maintainers—and LLMs—can combine with binaries and product media to preserve working knowledge across generational hardware turnover.

talks.title: The Automation of Exploits: Will Eatherton on AI-Driven Security and the End of Obscurity
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The Automation of Exploits: Will Eatherton on AI-Driven Security and the End of Obscurity.
talks.summary:
Attackers Without Silos

Cisco SVP Will Eatherton tells Hardwear.io that LLM-assisted testing is merging firmware, hardware, and software expertise. Specialized attackers once relied on niche obscurity; models now propose cross-domain exploits spanning FPGA designs, board components, and embedded code.

Automated Exploit Pipelines

Cisco experiments chain vulnerability hypothesis, lab device configuration, traffic generation, and result validation—work that once took days per creative tester. Similar AI coding experiments refactor legacy C into Rust at large scale, raising both development and offensive automation stakes.

Hardware Knowledge Gaps

Eatherton notes LLMs know common software frameworks well but lack training depth on proprietary schematics and Verilog compared to Python. Near-term gains come from better context retrieval—pulling firmware libraries, power-controller datasheets, and design artifacts into multi-step reasoning.

Open Source Still Wins

Despite AI risks, he does not expect a retreat from open-source hardware or software like SONiC. Shared components reduce unique attack surface, and AI may push teams to replace bespoke SSL libraries with maintained open alternatives.

talks.summary:
Attack cost

Roman Korkikian discusses hacking a TPM on budget edge-server hardware using custom sensing boards and used oscilloscopes, estimating total equipment under $2,000 rather than commercial lab gear.

Methodology

Side-channel and fault attacks are a last-mile option after software and protocol exploitation fail. He entered via cryptography/math, then specialized in power-analysis and voltage-fault techniques that break implementations, not algorithms.

TPM trust

The talk argues you cannot always trust TPMs; concrete device implementations may leak keys through physical analysis even when the crypto primitives remain sound.

Mitigation reality

Firmware updates can add masking, blinding, and randomization, but hardware-only flaws may require chip replacement, and certification cycles can delay fixes by years even after disclosure.

talks.summary:
## Overview
Hardware researcher John McMaster recounts a Hardwear.io networking-night experiment with George Hotz's comma.ai—a DIY driver-assistance stack that taps a car's CAN bus.

## How Comma.ai Works
Unlike commercial Waymo or Zoox vehicles, comma.ai intercepts CAN traffic after physical access to wiring. Code from GitHub plus a human "driver in the loop" enables semi-autonomous driving—McMaster dubs it "AI Jesus."

## Field Testing Reality
During qualification runs the system nearly steered into a pole on a left turn, requiring manual override. McMaster notes it is assistance, not full autonomy. A 12-volt reset left his infotainment dead—trade-offs of hacking production vehicles.

## Takeaways
Consumer self-driving hacks blur safety, liability, and hardware tinkering. Treat comma.ai as experimental ADAS requiring constant human supervision.

talks.title: Beyond the Hype: Guanxing on Exploiting Crypto Phones and the Evolution of Security Research
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Beyond the Hype: Guanxing on Exploiting Crypto Phones and the Evolution of Security Research.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this post-talk interview, security researcher Gwen Chen (referred to at the end as Guangcheng) from CertiK discusses his research into exploiting crypto phones and Ethereum wallets with interviewer Meltem Ozsoy (Intuitive Surgical) and a co-interviewer. The discussion covers his live demonstration of a USB-based exploit, the role of generative AI in reverse engineering, architectural flaws in crypto phones, and how researchers select emerging hardware and Web3 targets.

### Key Topics
- **Live Exploit Demos**: Chen reflected on delivering a live hardware exploit via USB to compromise an Ethereum wallet/phone. Because the attack utilized a physical USB connection rather than wireless vectors like Bluetooth or network connections, it was stable enough for a live stage demonstration.
- **Impact of AI on Security Research**: Chen broke down how tools like ChatGPT accelerated his reverse engineering workflow. Tasks like reverse engineering complex functions that previously took months were solved almost instantly by AI. However, he noted AI "took the fun" out of the research process, making the researcher feel like an agent being directed rather than an explorer, while stressing that domain knowledge in areas like TrustZone and boot ROMs is still mandatory to identify AI hallucinations and steer inquiries accurately.
- **Crypto Phone Architecture and Vendor Shortcuts**: The core premise of crypto phones is securing transactions and keys in trusted execution environments or hardware enclaves rather than regular userland Android space. While major manufacturers implement robust protections, smaller vendors often lack access to proprietary SDKs and relationships with chipset makers (e.g., Qualcomm, MediaTek) or Google, leading them to cut corners and downgrade security.
- **Target Selection in Web3**: Chen explained that the Web3 hardware ecosystem evolves so rapidly—ranging from hardware wallets and crypto POS terminals to DePIN devices and crypto phones—that new targets present themselves constantly without needing extensive searching.

### Technical Details
- **Exploit Vector**: Chen conducted a boot ROM exploitation delivered over USB to extract unencrypted keys from the crypto phone's Ethereum wallet in under a month.
- **Hardware Isolation vs. Boot ROM Flaws**: Chen highlighted that while a boot ROM exploit is severe, it does not automatically necessitate total system compromise if defense-in-depth is present. For example, Apple mitigated the "checkmate" boot ROM vulnerability using an isolated Secure Enclave Processor (SEP). Similarly, crypto phone vendors can utilize isolated secure chips or additional Android application-level obstacles to prevent access to keys even during low-level execution compromises.

### Takeaways
- Consumers and researchers should look beyond vendor marketing hype and white papers when evaluating crypto phones.
- Device trustworthiness should be judged by independent external evaluations, transparent bug bounty programs, responsible disclosure channels, and vendor reputation.
- Moving forward, Chen plans to shift focus toward more challenging hardware targets featuring newer technologies, such as hardware wallets incorporating iris biometric scanning.

talks.title: Reverse Engineering A Ledger Nano X Hardware Implant
talks.teaser: Traces how a tampered Ledger Nano X wallet hid a cellular-connected implant that captured recovery seeds.
talks.summary:
Joe Grand describes a case that began when a buyer in Thailand opened a cheap Ledger Nano X, purchased only for its battery, and found extra wiring and a smaller battery inside. He places this within hardware espionage, where legitimate devices are modified after they leave the factory and then resold. He compares it with earlier cases involving Treasure wallets, where swapped chips produced predictable keys, and with the 2020 Ledger customer data leak, which was followed by mailed devices carrying a USB drive that harvested seeds.

The middle of the talk covers his own investigation. He bought several units from third-party sellers on a marketplace, found that they also carried implants hidden under epoxy, and traced the added circuitry. The implant tapped the SPI lines between the secure element and the display, and it included a cellular module. Grand dumped the flash over SWD with OpenOCD, then read an embedded SIM with smart card tools, which showed a data-only subscription first registered in the Netherlands. Firmware analysis suggested the implant watched for the 26 letters shown during seed setup, stored them, and sent them over the cellular network.

He closes by covering follow-up work and coordination with Ledger, which recommends buying only from authorized resellers and comparing devices against known-good photos. His takeaway is that hardware provenance matters, and that attackers keep revising their implants as defenses change.

talks.title: Security Analysis Of Bluetooth Channel Sounding Protocol And Implementations
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Security Analysis Of Bluetooth Channel Sounding Protocol And Implementations.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security consultant Sultan analyzes the Bluetooth Channel Sounding protocol, introduced in Bluetooth 6.0 to provide secure distance bounding and high-precision ranging. While traditionally distance bounding has leveraged Ultra-Wideband (UWB) or relied on insecure Bluetooth RSSI and Angle of Arrival (AoA) techniques, Channel Sounding aims to deliver secure distance estimates using existing 2.4 GHz radio hardware without substantial cost increases. The technology is primarily targeted at access control systems such as phone-as-a-key for automotive and building entry.

### Key Topics
- **Ranging Modes**: The core specification defines Mode 1 (packet-based round-trip time of flight), Mode 2 (multicarrier phase-based ranging across 72 channels), and Mode 3 (a combination of both). Mode 0 measures crystal frequency offsets between initiator and reflector.
- **Packet-Based Ranging (Mode 1)**: Employs CS sync packets with 32-bit access addresses and optional 32-to-128 bit sounding or random sequences generated by an AES-based pseudo-random number generator (PRNG). This gives 32 to 160 bits of pseudo-random data per packet, preventing simple early-response spoofing.
- **Phase-Based Ranging (Mode 2)**: Measures phase shift and amplitude variations across multiple frequencies in the 2.4 GHz band to infer time of flight via phase slope. Because unmodulated tones carry little entropy, it relies on a single-bit pseudo-random "extension slot" per step where a tone may or may not be transmitted.
- **Multipath Handling Algorithms**: To separate direct line-of-sight paths from multipath reflections, implementations analyze the sparse frequency response using Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT), the Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC) algorithm, or trained neural networks.

### Technical Details & Implementation Flaws
Although Channel Sounding contains primitives intended for security, Sultan identifies critical architectural and implementation deficiencies across major vendor SDKs (TI, Nordic Semiconductor, NXP, and Silicon Labs):
1. **Lack of Specification Mandates**: The Bluetooth specification defines measurement primitives but leaves the method of combining data and calculating final distance to vendors. It also fails to mandate how security signals should be validated.
2. **Precision vs. Security Mismatch**: Packet-based ranging offers strong cryptographic protection against spoofing but suffers from extremely poor distance precision (~37.5 meters per sample period at common 4 MHz sampling rates) due to narrow channel bandwidth. Conversely, phase-based ranging delivers the necessary centimeter-level precision but has minimal entropy.
3. **Discarding Security Primitives**: In practice, vendor SDKs prioritize phase-based measurements and either omit, disable by default, or discard packet-based estimates. None of the examined implementations cross-validate phase measurements against packet time-of-flight.
4. **Ignored Extension Slots**: While hardware measures extension slots and reports their presence/absence over the Host Controller Interface (HCI), higher-layer SDK stacks completely discard extension slot data, leaving phase-based ranging vulnerable to tone-injection and phase-manipulation attacks.
5. **Absence of NATAM**: The Normalized Attack Detector Metric (NATAM), designed to detect Early Detect Late Commit (EDLC) attacks via cross-correlation or harmonic analysis, is optional in the specification and was not implemented by any evaluated vendor.

### Takeaways
Despite marketing claims promoting Channel Sounding as a secure ranging solution, current real-world implementations take the path of least resistance. Vendors default to unverified phase-based ranging for high precision while ignoring extension slots and omitting NATAM. Consequently, existing implementations fail to provide true secure distance bounding against active RF adversaries.

talks.title: NL 2025: Watch Out! A Security Case Study Of A COROS Sports Watch
talks.teaser: Shows how a popular COROS sports watch leaks data, exposes account tokens and crashes over Bluetooth Low Energy.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a widely worn COROS sports watch and asks what an attacker within Bluetooth range could do without physical access. The research found that the watch uses legacy Just Works pairing and adds no application-layer encryption, so its traffic can be eavesdropped on or altered. On Android, the companion app skips bonding entirely, which allowed an impersonated fake watch to capture the phone's account API token without any user interaction.

The presenter also showed that the watch accepts injected notifications while disconnected and can be made to reset or trigger a find-my-device alert. Blackbox fuzzing with Radamsa found two inputs that crash the watch. One came from a malformed notification structure, and the other came from a short message that caused an integer underflow and an out-of-bounds read. Firmware was obtained from the HTTP-based update process, and reversing the bootloader in Ghidra with SVD files revealed a second CPU and the firmware parsing logic.

Disclosure was slow, with fixes initially scheduled months away. After the advisories were published, a tech journalist's coverage added public pressure, and the vendor confirmed that all of its devices were affected and moved to prioritize the fixes. The takeaway for practitioners is that wearables with weak Bluetooth pairing can leak health and location data, and that vendor response timelines are worth scrutinising.

talks.title: NL 2025: Glitching Google's TV Streamer From Adb To Root
talks.teaser: Niek Timmers examines NL 2025: Glitching Google's TV Streamer From Adb To Root.
talks.summary:
### Overview

Nick Tmers from Railize presents a fault injection attack on Google's TV Streamer, demonstrating how electromagnetic glitches can corrupt CPU instructions to bypass kernel security checks and escalate privileges from an unprivileged ADB shell to root. Despite achieving a root shell, the attack is ultimately limited by SELinux enforcement.

### Key Topics

**Reconnaissance & Access**
- Google TV Streamer uses a quad-core ARM CPU at 1.8 GHz with DDR memory, eMMC storage, and external Wi-Fi/Ethernet chips
- Security posture similar to Pixel 9: secure boot, Android kernel hardening, and trusted execution environment (but no external Titan security chip)
- ADB debugging enabled via developer options; custom unprivileged code executable via Android Studio
- Firmware downloads obtained by interfacing with Google's OTA servers, yielding unencrypted boot and system partitions
- Kernel source and debug symbols publicly available from Google, including generic kernel image (GKI) with matching SHA-1 hash

**Fault Injection Setup**
- Electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) technique using a Keysite glitch device to generate high-current pulses through a coil
- Setup: XYZ stage for probe positioning, USB control for power cycling resets, minimal wiring
- Target: corrupting CPU instructions during execution to bypass software security models

**Characterization Phase**
- Two-phase scanning of chip surface: coarse scan (10 power levels across 20×20 grid, ~40 minutes) identifies responsive locations; fine-grained scan targets those locations
- Custom test code runs in user-space loop, incrementing counter to 10,000; altered counter values written to disk indicate successful faults
- Fault models observed: instruction skipping, instruction corruption (changing operands or entire instruction), bit flips in instruction encoding
- Different sensitive locations per CPU core (quad-core dependency confirms CPU targeting)

**Privilege Escalation Attack**
- Target: setuid syscall's capability check for CAP_SETUID, which blocks unprivileged processes from changing UID to root
- Attack code continuously issues setuid(0,0,0) syscalls; glitch injection bypasses kernel capability check at random power levels
- Success indicated by process spawning root-owned Telnetd; attacker connects via Telnet for root shell
- Attack timeline: minutes to ~1 hour execution time despite Android boot overhead

**Results & Limitations**
- Successfully achieved root shell access with `id` command confirmation
- SELinux still enforced; cannot read /proc/kmem or flash memory (LSM hooks intact)
- Ability to read /proc/syslog by bypassing its permission checks suggests other syscall attacks possible
- Full device compromise not achieved; boot-level attacks identified as more powerful alternative

### Technical Details

- **Instruction Corruption Example**: Single bit flip in ARM64 instruction encoding (e.g., `0x21` → `0x20`) changes instruction semantics (operand or operation type)
- **Fault Parameters**: Power/current magnitude drives EM field strength; precise timing and location required for reproducibility
- **Kernel Protection Layers**: Capability checks, SELinux hooks, and Linux Security Modules; fault injection circumvents capability checks but not SELinux
- **Device Reset**: USB power cycling used for state recovery after error conditions

### Takeaways

- Google TV Streamer's CPU vulnerable to EM fault injection despite >1 GHz clock speeds
- Runtime privilege escalation via fault injection feasible on Android with ≤1 hour attack windows
- Software security architectures fail when executing on hardware lacking fault injection countermeasures
- SELinux provides secondary defense that withstood tested attack; full compromise likely requires kernel exploitation or alternative attack vectors
- Google and MediaTek acknowledged vulnerability as inherent to platform; not device-specific
- Boot-time attacks likely more efficient than runtime attacks for full compromise
- Demo available at Keysite booth showing live exploitation on unmodified Google TV Streamer running latest firmware

talks.title: NL 2025: [Keynote] Towards End-User Verifiable Silicon
talks.teaser: Presents infrared inspection of soldered chips as a way to verify silicon in finished products without destroying them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues for higher assurance silicon, borrowing the idea of structural correctness from projects such as Fiat Crypto, a formally proven compiler for elliptic curve code. It contrasts this with chip buyers today, who must rely on labels, certifications and designer claims. The speaker walks through supply chain risks, including gray markets, customs checkpoints and tampered products returned to distributors, and shows a decapped chip whose internals did not match its markings.

The central technique is IRIS, infrared in situ verification. It images a chip through its exposed backside after the chip is soldered to a board, so the device under inspection can still be used. It works on flip-chip and wafer-level packages with thinned, lightly doped substrates, but not on plastic-molded packages. Inexpensive microscope cameras with the infrared filter removed can do basic imaging, and a CNC-controlled rig can produce repeatable reference images. Example images show a touchscreen controller's converter channels and standard cells from a 130 nm design, and the speaker notes that electrical scan chain tests can be paired with optical checks.

The talk closes with open silicon. It argues that mature 28 nm nodes make open-source tape-outs economically viable, and describes adding an open RISC-V core and a software-defined I/O block to a commercial chip, along with RTL that allows simulation-based debugging. Practical takeaways include asking manufacturers for inspectable packaging, building shared databases of chip images, and helping find bugs in open designs.

talks.title: NL 2024: EL3XIR: Fuzzing COTS Secure Monitors
talks.teaser: Marcel Busch analyzes NL 2024: EL3XIR: Fuzzing COTS Secure Monitors.
talks.summary:
Overview: ARM TrustZone forms the security backbone of mobile devices. TrustZone-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) facilitate security-sensitive tasks like user authentication and disk encryption. As such, bugs in the TEE software stack may compromise the entire system’s integrity. Unfortunately, modern dynamic analysis techniques (like fuzzing) typically used to identify and eliminate those bugs cannot be effectively applied to TEE components. In this talk, we introduce EL3XIR, a framework to effectively rehost and fuzz the secure monitor firmware layer of proprietary TrustZone-based TEEs. Wh
Details: ile other approaches have focused on naively rehosting or fuzzing Trusted Applications or the TEE OS, EL3XIR targets the highly-privileged but underexplored secure monitor and its unique challenges. Secure monitors expose complex functionality through diverse secure monitor calls that may depend on multiple peripherals. In this talk, we share how we overcame these challenges regarding input injection and peripheral emulation for several targets to find a total of 34 bugs, out of which 17 were classified as security critical. Affected vendors confirmed 14 of these bugs, and as a result, EL3XIR was assigned six CVEs.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Understanding Physics To Break AES With Side-channel Hardware -Stephan & Roman
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for NL 2023 | Understanding Physics To Break AES With Side-channel Hardware -Stephan & Roman.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, embedded systems/electronics designer Matthew and security researcher Roman examine side-channel hardware setups from an electronic design perspective. Originating from Matthew's critique of Roman's test setup while repeating a side-channel attack on a Jade crypto wallet, the talk bridges physical electronics engineering with cryptographic side-channel analysis. The speakers demonstrate how wiring, decoupling capacitors, probe noise, and power supplies directly impact correlation power analysis (CPA) on hardware AES implementations, targeting an ESP32 microcontroller with a built-in cryptographic engine.

### Key Topics
- **Impact of Wires and Inductance**: Evaluating how wire length and loop area introduce parasitic inductance, which attenuates high-frequency current content and degrades correlation quality.
- **Decoupling Capacitors**: Investigating the common practice of removing decoupling capacitors to prevent high-frequency operational currents from bypassing external current-measurement instrumentation.
- **Target Clock vs. Leakage Bandwidth**: Analyzing filtering cutoffs to discover the optimal frequency band for recovering AES keys, contrasting system clock speed with cryptographic leakage frequencies.
- **Measurement Hardware and Ground Loops**: Comparing measurement instruments (differential probes, current probes, LISNs, shunt resistors) and solving ground loops and oscilloscope input noise.
- **Low-Cost Custom Hardware Solutions**: Designing accessible, budget-friendly low-side and inline side-channel acquisition hardware.

### Technical Details
- **Wiring and Parasitic Inductance**: Testing signal transmission from 1 MHz to 500 MHz confirmed that larger wiring loops increase inductance and introduce up to 10 dB of high-frequency attenuation. In time-domain AES measurements on the ESP32, connecting the target directly via solder joints preserved high-frequency spikes and allowed key recovery at 50,000 traces. Introducing just 2 cm wires significantly damped these transients and forced the Pearson correlation to require far more traces for successful key recovery.
- **Decoupling Capacitors**: Because decoupling capacitors sit near the microcontroller to supply transient switching currents locally, leaving them populated shunts the high frequencies away from the power supply sensing path. While slow operations like ciphertext transfers remained detectable with capacitors present, the actual AES key could not be recovered within 300,000 traces without removing them. However, removing decoupling capacitors means long supply wires can cause severe voltage dips, potentially causing target reboots.
- **Bandwidth and Filtering**: Even though the ESP32 CPU runs at 160 MHz, low-pass filtering experiments revealed that the highest Pearson correlation coefficient and clearest key separation occurred when low-pass filtering from DC to 95 MHz. Adding content between 95 MHz and 100 MHz degraded correlation, proving that high-cost gigahertz measurement equipment is unnecessary.
- **Noise Optimization and Instrumentation**: Environmental noise, power supply ripple, and probe self-noise hinder trace quality. Standard bench power supplies performed poorly compared to clean battery setups or power supplies conditioned with low-dropout (LDO) regulators. Current probes (limited to ~100 MHz and introducing ~75 µA RMS noise) and differential probes (flat response dominated by ~28 µA RMS noise) performed worse in correlation attacks than custom pre-amplified boards.
- **Custom Acquisition Hardware**: To eliminate ground loops and drown out the oscilloscope's internal noise floor without requiring averaging across acquisitions, Matthew developed two low-cost hardware platforms:
  1. *Low-side board ($125)*: Integrates target power delivery, an on-board shunt resistor, and a two-stage op-amp amplifier with potentiometers for variable gain, achieving up to 1 GHz bandwidth.
  2. *Inline/high-side board ($25)*: Designed to connect in-line across power traces using a balun transformer to isolate DC from high-frequency components, paired with RF amplifiers, avoiding ground loops.
- **EM Side-Channel Applicability**: Addressing an audience question, Matthew explained that removing decoupling capacitors also benefits electromagnetic (EM) side-channel attacks by enlarging the high-frequency current loop path, effectively turning it into a larger loop antenna that radiates stronger EM signals.

### Takeaways
To achieve fast, reliable, and low-cost side-channel key recovery, practitioners should eliminate jumper wires by soldering directly, desolder local decoupling capacitors, power targets via batteries or LDO-filtered supplies, and amplify signals prior to the oscilloscope. Hardware AES on chips like the ESP32 can be broken efficiently using inexpensive secondhand oscilloscopes and custom front-end boards without spending thousands of dollars on high-end differential probes.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Automated Fault Injection Attacks On Embedded Devices
talks.teaser: Details how electromagnetic fault injection can hijack automotive microcontroller firmware without prior knowledge of the code.
talks.summary:
The talk covers automated electromagnetic fault injection against automotive electronic control units. The team first tried voltage glitching, but it required heavy board modification and temperature control, so they switched to EMFI, which needs no changes to the board. Their main target was a gateway ECU built on an automotive-grade NXP microcontroller. Published attacks on similar chips did not work on the real device, and program counter corruption tricks that suit ARM were much harder on PowerPC.

The attack used the standard diagnostic flashing process. Its unlock step relies on repair shop secrets that have leaked publicly, and the erase step happens before the new image is verified, so an attacker could reach about 4 MB of flash with a jump. Exception handlers on this device printed register dumps over UART, which gave the team feedback on each injection. A genetic search algorithm used that feedback to tune coil position, pulse duration, voltage, timing and memory state. It found a working program counter corruption after roughly 10,000 injections on average, at about five per second. The resulting code execution could read the bootloader and re-enable JTAG through configuration records.

The setup cost about 5,000 and worked on five targets from three manufacturers across three architectures. The lesson for practitioners is that fault injection can be cheaper and more automatable than expected when a target emits useful feedback. Suggested mitigations include memory protection unit write or execute rules, running the bootloader inside the HSM, and authenticating every firmware write rather than relying on a single validity flag.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Hacking A Smart Doorbell: An IoT Hacking Guide
talks.teaser: Shows how a smart doorbell's Bluetooth Low Energy setup traffic and unencrypted video stream can be sniffed and abused.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through hacking a cheap smart doorbell that offers Wi-Fi and Bluetooth Low Energy, using a neighbour on the home network as the threat model. It begins with the companion Android app: decompiling it and using Frida to bypass SSL pinning showed encrypted API traffic, and certificate validation held for the main domain. Attention then turns to Bluetooth Low Energy, covering the stack from HCI through ATT and GATT, and how services are enumerated with nRF Connect and Bettercap.

Sniffing the setup session is the core of the attack. Android HCI snoop logs serve as a reference, and a Sniffle receiver on low-cost TI boards captures the pairing traffic over the air. Filtering the ATT write requests exposes the Wi-Fi network name, password and an account name, sent as JSON split across packets because pairing used no link-layer encryption. The camera's Wi-Fi traffic is also unencrypted: ring notifications go over HTTP and the video stream over UDP as JPEG frames, which a short Python script can extract and which can be replaced with other images.

The closing advice is to place the doorbell on a separate Wi-Fi network and set it up somewhere trusted, since its proprietary firmware is hard to change. In Q&A, the speaker noted that the Bluetooth service shuts down after setup, and an audience member said similar devices also send credentials in plain text.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Attacking Vehicle Fleet Management Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed telematics boxes and an unauthenticated MQTT fleet backend let attackers track and control vehicles.
talks.summary:
Two researchers describe a side project that began in 2020 to examine internet-connected automotive embedded devices for flaws that could be exploited remotely at scale. Most of the roughly 18 devices they tested had serious, easy-to-find issues. The talk focuses on two telematics control units used for fleet management, which the speakers said could affect tens of thousands of vehicles.

The first unit, a box sold by a Chinese vendor and installed in heavy machinery such as cranes and trucks, could be rooted physically through an exposed USB connector. Its firmware had no binary protections. The bundled MQTT client pointed to a broker with no authentication, where a binary protocol carried GPS, fuel, and engine data tied to SIM identifiers. Anyone could publish to any vehicle's topic, impersonating vehicles or the backend. The speakers described possible CAN injection and malicious firmware updates but did not test them. Vendor responses were slow, and the flaw was reportedly still present at the last check.

The second case started from exposed brokers found with Shodan and Censys. Documentation and domain names helped identify one fleet-management vendor. Firmware was pulled from an update URL seen in traffic, revealing a command handler that ran without a token check. An ID derived from epoch time let the team achieve code execution on thousands of devices, with access to live video, tire pressure monitoring, and engine immobilization. Disclosure was still open when the talk was given, so the vendor's name was withheld. The takeaway is that fleet backends should require authentication and that exposed IoT services deserve regular external checks.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Basebanheimer: Now I Am Become Death, The Destroyer Of Chains -Daniel Komaromy
talks.teaser: Walks through cellular baseband exploitation on Samsung and MediaTek modems, from a heap overflow to a Linux kernel pivot.
talks.summary:
The talk covers cellular baseband research aimed at building complete exploit chains, from a zero-click trigger in the modem through to the application processor, on newer Samsung Shannon and MediaTek Dimensity chipsets. For Samsung, the speaker described a heap overflow in LTE session management, where traffic flow template packet filter components were limited only by a formula while a fixed-size array could hold fewer entries. A hidden debug mode that records heap events and produces RAM dumps helped with debugging, and network-controlled filter allocation served as heap shaping. The usual unlinking technique did not fit, because the overflow writes pointers rather than chosen values.

Samsung's user-space radio interface daemon also produced stack and heap overflows quickly, though hardened allocators make them hard to weaponize. On MediaTek Dimensity, the move to a new instruction set required a decompiler plugin and QEMU support before bug hunting. A layer 2 GPRS radio link control bug came from unlimited reassembly of containers across messages, and the vendor advisory described it inaccurately. The talk also explored a direct route into the Linux kernel through shared-memory ring buffers, where an integer wrap and attacker-controlled offsets allowed arbitrary reads and writes. That is effectively full coverage on 32-bit kernels, and on 64-bit kernels scanning for targets was practical. A demo closed the talk.

Several chains remained under embargo or unfinished, so the speaker presented them as work in progress. The main takeaway is that baseband bugs are often reachable through specification gaps and shared-memory bookkeeping, and that public tooling and debugging aids have made these modems far easier to study.

talks.title: USA 2023 | Building A Modern Bluetooth Sniffer
talks.teaser: Shows how to sniff all Bluetooth channels at once with software-defined radio and feed the decoded packets into Wireshark.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a practical limit of Bluetooth sniffing. Narrowband software-defined radios hop between channels and miss traffic, while wideband capture hardware is expensive. The speaker presents a multi-channel approach using a Blade RF device, whose newer firmware covers enough spectrum to watch all Bluetooth channels at the same time. He also introduces a tool that integrates with Wireshark, so captured packets appear directly under the interface list.

Much of the talk explains the signal processing behind the tool. Raw IQ samples are split into individual channels with a polyphase channelizer, bursts are detected by amplitude, and frequency demodulation with offset correction turns each burst into bits. Without a connection's access address, the decoder finds packet starts by checking whether the length field in the BLE header matches the burst length. To keep up with the sample rate, the channelizer uses SIMD fixed-point arithmetic and a GPU-accelerated FFT library. The speaker said this let a modern laptop decode all 80 classic channels and all 40 BLE channels in real time. He also noted that per-radio physical characteristics can be plotted to track individual devices.

The live demo showed Bluetooth advertising packets, including some unencrypted BLE traffic. The speaker closed by describing unfinished work: classic Bluetooth support, Windows builds, and channel hopping for cheaper radios that cannot cover the full band. A practitioner who wants to try this today can install the tool with a supported radio, though its limits on narrower radios matter for planning.

talks.title: Exploring chip decaping techniques for silicon die inspection and reverse engineering
talks.teaser: Shows how hot air can soften a chip's plastic package so its silicon die can be exposed for inspection.
talks.summary:
Chip secrets are often locked inside their packages, so the silicon die and the circuits on it cannot be seen directly. The talk focuses on removing the die from plastic packages, a step needed before the silicon can be examined closely.

Two approaches are compared. Very strong acid works but is dangerous to handle. Heating the package with a hot air tool is far cheaper and simpler, and it is the method demonstrated. The plastic casing is heated until it is hot enough to weaken, then the package is cracked open by hand to reveal the die.

Once the die is exposed, the speaker cleans off the remaining material and shows the silicon sitting in the opened package. The takeaway for practitioners is that a basic heat source can expose a die for visual inspection and reverse engineering without resorting to acid.

talks.title: Affordable EMFI Attacks Against Modern IoT Chips by Davide Toldo
talks.teaser: Shows how a low-cost electromagnetic fault injection rig can skip instructions on a modern IoT chip with secure boot.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that modern IoT chips with closed debug ports, secure boot and flash encryption still have a gap. Electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) can disrupt a chip from outside and skip checks even when the code itself is sound. The speaker presents it as an introductory walkthrough for newcomers who want a reproducible EMFI setup on a budget, and explains why a pulse must be placed accurately in both time and space.

The build starts with a cheap XY positioning stage, where a belt-driven 3D printer or drawing robot is preferred over lead-screw designs because of backlash. An inexpensive FPGA board handles the delay generator, with a Raspberry Pi Pico or ChipWhisperer as alternatives. Pulsers range from a commercial unit that reaches higher voltage to the open-source PicoEMP. Custom hardware reset and SMB-connected breakouts, plus a control script that logs results to CSV for 2D mapping, complete the rig. On a recent chip, a test loop showed instruction skips in specific die regions, while brownout detection and USB polling noise complicated the work.

The takeaway is that the entry cost is modest and that deployed devices may be exposed if an attacker has physical access and time. Practitioners should check whether this attack fits their threat model. If glitches do not appear, a higher-voltage pulser may be needed, and even well-written code cannot fully defend against this class of attack.

talks.title: BreakMi: Reversing, Exploiting & Fixing Fitness Tracking Ecosystems by M. Casagrande & D. Antonioli
talks.teaser: Reverse engineers Xiaomi and Fitbit tracker Bluetooth protocols and shows how pairing and session flaws enable device takeover.
talks.summary:
Fitness trackers pair with a phone companion app over Bluetooth Low Energy, and the app relays their data to a vendor backend over Wi-Fi. This talk assesses the Xiaomi and Fitbit ecosystems, whose application-layer protocols are proprietary and undocumented. The researchers captured Bluetooth traffic with HCI snoop logs and Wireshark, decompiled the Android companion apps, used dynamic instrumentation to match captured packets with values in memory, and intercepted the app's Wi-Fi traffic to map backend endpoints.

In the Xiaomi devices tested, link-layer encryption was disabled and the application layer offered no confidentiality or integrity. The older pairing version sent the pairing key in clear text behind a weak button confirmation. The newer version relied on a public key shared across the whole ecosystem, and its authentication challenge could be replayed, with only the app authenticating to the tracker. The speakers demonstrated dropping, impersonation and man-in-the-middle attacks from nearby, plus a remote attack from a malicious Android app that shares the phone's BLE channel and can trigger an unauthenticated factory reset, enabling device takeover. The Fitbit Charge 2 fared better, with link-layer security enabled and MAC-based authentication, but its real-time mode was unencrypted and its pairing was replayable, which still allowed impersonation.

The toolkit is open source, and the authors reported the issues to both vendors. Xiaomi classified the problem as a lack of encryption and reportedly shipped new firmware, while Google acknowledged the findings and released a fix. The proposed countermeasures are user-indicated pairing, authenticated encryption keyed with the pairing key, and enabling BLE link-layer security. The takeaway is that vendor-specific app-layer protocols should not be trusted to protect wearable data on their own.

talks.title: Keynote |The Microarchitectures That I Saw And The Ones That I Hope To One Day See by Rodrigo Branco
talks.teaser: Recounts CPU side-channel disclosures and vendor responses, drawing lessons on hidden assumptions and system composition.
talks.summary:
In this keynote, Rodrigo Branco looks back on about fifteen years of CPU security work, with more attention to failures and frustrations than to wins. He argues that most serious flaws come from two sources: assumptions that abstraction layers make about the components beneath them, and the mistaken belief that individually secure parts remain secure when combined. For unfamiliar systems, he suggests listing what you don't know, then building tooling to answer those questions.

The middle of the talk recounts how side-channel concerns were handled inside a major chip vendor. A casual answer given to students in 2007, that cache leaks were a software problem, hardened into internal policy and resisted later challenges. He describes pushing for a clear position on kernel address randomization after a TSX-based bypass, the 2017 research that used cache side channels against browser ASLR, and an early public disclosure in 2018 triggered by a competitor's patch. Other cases include a report on the management engine dismissed as unexploitable until the research team was reorganized, and cloud mitigations that had been broken for years without anyone noticing.

He closes by urging basic checks, such as re-running published proofs of concept, and by noting that bugs in hardware that cannot be patched tend to persist. He criticizes marketing-driven vendor responses and legal pressure around disclosure, and encourages researchers to keep probing complex systems, since skills carry across targets.

talks.title: Bypass NXP LPC-Family Debug Check with Voltage Fault Injection by Waleed AlZamil and Bandar Alharbi
talks.teaser: Shows how a voltage glitch during power-on defeats the debug lock on an NXP LPC1343 microcontroller.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the code read protection (CRP) mechanism in NXP LPC microcontrollers, which decides at boot whether the debug interface stays enabled. The speakers walk through the protection levels, the configuration word that sets them, and where the boot code checks that word. They note that earlier 2017 research used voltage fault injection to reach flash through the ISP bootloader, which led them to target the debug lock instead.

Their test setup used an LPC1343 driven by a glitch generator and a probe, with the decoupling capacitor on the core supply removed to make the glitch easier to deliver. Attempts that timed the glitch from a reset trigger did not work. Moving the trigger to a power-on cycle produced a successful glitch. The team used it to re-enable the debug interface, read back the stored CRP3 value, and showed the attack against the CRP1, CRP2 and CRP3 levels. They also compared the boot code across other LPC families, found a similar mechanism, and assumed comparable checks exist there.

The practical takeaway is that a debug lock enforced by a boot-time check can be undone by a well-timed voltage glitch, so hardware read protection has to account for fault injection. The speakers said they contacted NXP, which discussed the findings with them and was professional in its response. The session closed with audience questions about how the glitch was triggered and whether the vendor planned mitigations.

talks.title: Practical Invasive Attacks, How Hardware is Hacked For Compatible Product Creation by Thomas Olivier
talks.teaser: Shows how an invasive reverse engineering team probes a secure chip's ROM to clone printer cartridge electronics.
talks.summary:
Compatible printer cartridge makers need to understand the secure chips inside original cartridges. The speaker framed this as a threat model in which the main barrier is how long an attacker needs to clone a device. These chips are packaged black boxes with no datasheet, pinout or architecture reference, so the work starts from zero. The target had analog blocks, a digital CPU, flash, ROM and RAM spread across five metal layers.

The team delayered the die by mechanical polishing, imaged each layer with a scanning microscope, stitched the images and rebuilt the standard cell library to read the netlist. An angled polish exposed the ROM bits, and the extracted dump looked unencrypted, yet it still did not yield readable strings or recognisable code. The shield over the chip blocked direct probing, so the team used focused ion beam rewiring to reach internal signals, then microprobed them and found that the ROM boots before the flash. Netlist tracing exposed memory select logic, a control path into the instruction register, and a shield sensor whose input could be tied to supply voltage, disabling the shield and two other countermeasures.

Full analysis stayed out of reach because the ROM address scrambling and an apparently custom instruction set remained unresolved. Next steps were to simulate the fetch circuitry and rebuild the datasheet. The speaker's takeaway is that a shield is only one layer, that no chip resists unlimited invasive effort, and that certification schemes need better ways to assess reverse engineering attacks.

talks.teaser: Explains how Bluetooth LE link-layer relay attacks defeat proximity-based keyless entry, and how to mitigate them.
talks.summary:
Proximity-based keyless systems, including car key fobs, smart locks, building access controls and some laptops and phones, unlock when a trusted token is nearby. They estimate distance from signal strength, time of flight or phase measurements. Signal-strength checks are easy to fool, and ranging schemes without a cryptographic distance check can also be beaten. Relaying traffic between a token and a lock makes both devices believe they are close together, even when they are far apart.

The talk reviews earlier relay approaches against Bluetooth Low Energy. GAP-layer relays used standard host APIs, HCI-level relays bypassed the host stack, and analog relays carried the whole 2.4 GHz band but added latency and range limits. The focus is a link-layer relay, in which one device acts as a master toward the real peripheral and as a slave toward the real central, forwarding link-layer packets. Added latency can be hidden by choosing a shorter connection interval on one side. Encryption is the main obstacle, because control packets are encrypted and both sides must keep matching counters. The attacker must therefore find when connection updates take effect, using traffic analysis and empty packets to probe timing. A live demonstration relayed an unlock request over distance to a Tesla Model Y at short range.

The main mitigations are requiring user interaction before an unlock, and using secure ranging standards that verify distance cryptographically, which limits how far a relay can stretch the apparent distance. The practical takeaway is that signal-strength or unauthenticated timing checks alone should not protect valuable assets, since BLE relay attacks are practical.

talks.title: Keynote | Reverse Engineering Is Good For Soul by Travis Goodspeed | hardwear.io NL 2022
talks.teaser: Shares personal stories of reverse engineering, from smart card firmware dumps to a DIY wristwatch that doubles as a radio.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that reverse engineering is the work the speaker enjoys most, more than security itself, and that it is worth protecting from jobs that crowd it out. Travis Goodspeed recounts his career, including a stint in New York taking apart products and a factory line, and time working with Windows reverse engineer Jeff Chapel, whose publishing dropped off once he lacked the quiet to work. A nuclear engineer friend serves as a contrast: he stopped enjoying his job because he could not take on small, self-contained problems.

The technical examples come next. A 1998 report on Nagravision smart cards, released during litigation, described reading firmware through instruction fetches by placing needles on the chip, along with a buffer overflow in the card's input buffer. Goodspeed adapted that overflow to a modern USB smart card reader and published a Go client that dumps the reader's firmware. He also built a home chemistry setup for decapping and delayering chips, and wrote a ROM annotation tool called Mastermind. Separately, he described the 1997 dispute between AOL and MSN Messenger, in which an overflow in AOL's Oscar protocol client was used to survey which messenger users were running.

He closes with his own wristwatch project: a TI MSP430-based board that fits an original watch case, with amateur radio transmit, a frequency counter, and an on-watch disassembler. He urges listeners to keep reverse engineering in their lives and to protect the time needed to do it.

talks.title: Grinding Tractors To A Halt Growing Pains In Agricultural HardwareSecurity by Sick Codes hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Follows chip-off extraction of John Deere tractor firmware and exposed keys, showing how unencrypted embedded devices leak secrets.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with recent ransomware and extortion incidents hitting agriculture and food companies, including Colonial Pipeline, JBS Foods, a farmer cooperative and AGCO. From there it asks what happens to a manufacturer's embedded code once hardware leaves the factory, since used units circulate on resale sites and can be taken apart at home.

The research centres on a secondhand John Deere telematics gateway. Its NAND flash was removed with a hot air gun and read through a socket, then the file system was rebuilt in a Docker container. Findings included an engineering mode that could be switched on before login, a temporary folder not held in RAM, and plaintext databases holding a Wi-Fi password. A key pair for an MQTT setup was identical across devices; the vendor confirmed it was a development key left in production, though it was not in active use. A hardcoded repository login let the speaker download about 4,000 RPM packages before directory listing was disabled, and a leftover trash folder on one unit revealed the packages needed to rebuild the operating system on a Raspberry Pi.

The speaker closes by arguing that the minimal kit is cheap, that very few researchers examine agricultural equipment, and that secondhand chips may still hold customer data. The Q&A touched on right-to-repair, the vendor's response to the disclosures, and the later launch of a bug bounty program.

talks.title: Perimeter Breached! Hacking An Access Control System by Steve Povolny & Sam Quinn | hardwear.io USA
talks.teaser: Shows how a building access control panel was taken over through its serial, JTAG and web interface flaws to gain root and unlock doors.
talks.summary:
Trellix researchers Steve Povolny and Sam Quinn explain why they targeted access control systems, which they see as a single point of failure bridging physical and digital security. They bought a used Mercury-made panel whose marketing said it was approved for government facilities, then started with its circuit board. A four-pin port carried serial output that stopped during boot, and a 20-pin port looked like JTAG.

Using a J-Link debugger, they halted the processor, dumped the U-Boot bootloader and found a hard-coded boot delay of zero that blocked interrupting boot. Patching it gave them a bootloader shell and then a root shell over serial. A hardware watchdog that rebooted the board about every 15 seconds was disabled by flipping one bit in its mode register. The web interface ran CGI pages as root, and a hostname field reached a system call. Character filters were bypassed with tabs and curl, and that payload only ran at boot. A firmware upload diagnostic page skipped authentication and had a buffer overflow in signature-size parsing, which chained with the injection into unauthenticated remote code execution.

The team reported eight zero-days to the vendor. The two covered in the talk scored 9.0 and 10.0, and the vendor said other OEM partners using the boards are affected too. For the demo, they wrote a small program that called a kernel driver to hold door relays open. The takeaway is that certification claims say little about device security, and debug ports and default settings deserve close scrutiny.

talks.title: Breaking A Recent SoC’s Hardware AES Accelerator Using Body Biasing Injection by Karim M. Abdellatif
talks.teaser: Shows a low-cost body biasing injector faulting a recent SoC's hardware AES accelerator and recovering its key.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at body biasing injection, a fault injection technique that applies a high voltage through a needle touching the substrate of a decapped chip. The speaker notes it is rarely covered in the literature and is cheaper than laser attacks, though it still requires decapping. The earlier low-cost design was extended with a programmable voltage near 250 volts, both pulse polarities, microcontroller control and USB power.

A glitchable counter loop first confirmed that positive and negative pulses altered results at different spots on the surface. The target was a low-power SoC with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, built on 40 nm and used in hardware wallets. Power traces and a signal-to-noise leakage check identified the window where the AES accelerator ran. Early faults at 250 volts only corrupted the output communication. An external supply raised the effective voltage to about 500 volts, and tuning let the speaker fault AES in round nine with roughly 60 percent success.

With faulty ciphertexts from round nine, the speaker ran differential fault analysis and recovered the full AES key using about 10,000 trials. Practical notes covered damage risk: three chips were damaged, so the needle should be lifted before moving across the surface, and front-side decapping is harder. The main takeaway is that a cheap homemade injector can break a hardware AES accelerator. Future work includes testing more devices and checking how the technique affects unsecured elements and glitch detectors.

talks.title: Self-labeling Electronic Shelf Labels by Steffen Robertz | hardwear.io USA 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how electronic shelf labels can be torn down, decoded over their 433 MHz radio link, and forged or replayed.
talks.summary:
The talk examines electronic shelf labels, the e-ink price tags used in supermarkets and increasingly in hospitals and document storage. The speaker outlines the market growth and possible abuse, including blocking price updates, luring shoppers to malicious QR codes, and reusing cheap displays. The target was a tag from a common Chinese supplier, paired with a base station that converts Ethernet into a proprietary 433 MHz protocol.

The teardown covered the external flash, which held the image data, and an unlabelled microcontroller. Acid decapping exposed a die marking, and a unique-ID lookup pointed to an STM8 low-power part. Its SWIM debug header, found on the board, allowed flash readout, although protection was enabled. The FCC filings did not match the observed signal, which was FSK slightly off the stated frequency. Replaying a captured price update with an SDR restored an old price, so no replay protection existed. The speaker decoded the frame types and their run-length image compression, then rebuilt the protocol in GNU Radio to push a custom image onto a tag.

The main lesson is that the protocol had no authentication, integrity checks or real error correction, and that a custom radio protocol offers little protection when a cheap transceiver chip can capture it. Because tags do not reply to the sender, an attacker's range is mainly limited by transmit power. The speaker recommends encryption, authentication and error correction, and plans to publish the tools and firmware dumps.

talks.title: Unwanted Features: Finding & Exploiting An In ROM Buffer Overflow On The LPC55S69 by Laura Abbott
talks.teaser: Details a buffer overflow in an NXP boot ROM on a microcontroller and how it leads to code execution despite protections.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with why a company building servers chose the NXP LPC55S69 microcontroller as a hardware root of trust for measuring its software. Because the chip's boot ROM includes a firmware update parser for the SB2 format, the team had to decide whether that code could be trusted.

The core finding is that the ROM parser treats SB2 header fields as untrusted input. An integer underflow and a conditionally updated callback let a copy run past a global buffer, and an adjacent heap allocator variable gives the attacker control of the callback pointer. That redirects execution into ROM code, which the memory protection unit restricts, but an executable ROM patch area in SRAM sits at the end of the overflowed region. A stack canary, checked only during ISP mode, was bypassed by a single 512-byte write that overwrote it. The payload then disables the MPU and SAU. An attacker could read flash and roll back signed images, but keys and secure boot settings on a sealed device stayed protected. The unique device secret had not yet been locked at the time, which threatens DICE-based device identity.

NXP agreed to fix the issue in new silicon, but that takes time, so interim mitigations such as validating the header in code on the chip and checking signatures were weighed, with the caveat that signatures prove only authenticity. The team decided to write its own update mechanism instead. Takeaways include validating input at every boundary, recognizing that ROM bugs are hard to fix, and publishing ROM source so customers can audit it.

talks.title: Can you park a car in a classroom? | Phillippe Azalbert | hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Describes how a portable automotive test bench was built from scavenged ECUs, with sensor emulation and lessons for car security training.
talks.summary:
This talk from Quarks Lab explains why automotive security training benefits from a portable test bench, and how one was built. Modern cars run dozens of electronic control units over networks such as CAN and LIN, with a growing wireless attack surface. Bringing a real car to a training room is impractical, since few attendees can touch it at once and a triggered crash frame can lock the powertrain module until a manufacturer tool resets it.

The Car in a Box is a case sized to fit aboard a plane, holding ECUs from a scrapped vehicle wired to several networks, an infotainment unit with Bluetooth and cellular, and a control panel. The builders learned that some modules are immobilizer-enrolled and need a matching working car, that wake-up frames must be present, and that pin documentation should be located before wiring straight to pins instead of untangling harnesses. Sensors were emulated with an Arduino Mega using relays to ground, digital potentiometers for variable resistance, and a timer-driven clock for square signals, while a tyre pressure sensor was replayed with a software-defined radio. A Raspberry Pi touchscreen controls the simulation over serial.

Takeaways include that the same ECU weaknesses can span models and manufacturers, that some signals such as fuel level are averaged over about a minute, and that most microcontrollers are protected, so firmware recovery may need vendor hardware. Third-party diagnostic apps can reveal hidden manufacturer commands. The speaker also answered questions on costs, a build time of three to four weeks, and the role of UDS diagnostics.

talks.title: MoonBounce: Internals of the 3rd publicly known UEFI firmware implant | Mark Lechtik | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Traces how the MoonBounce UEFI implant hooks boot services to reach Windows user mode and links it to APT41.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Kaspersky's analysis of MoonBounce, a UEFI firmware implant found in the wild by the company's firmware scanning technology. The speaker explains the boot process the implant abuses, focusing on the DXE dispatcher stored in SPI flash, where the attackers patched the first bytes of several boot services functions with inline hooks. Each hook restores the original bytes after its first run and passes control on, so normal boot continues.

The infection chain is walked through in stages. An AllocatePool hook places shellcode in physical memory, and a CreateEventEx hook registers a callback for legacy boot so the payload can be mapped in that case as well. An ExitBootServices hook lets the implant survive into the Windows loader, where it hooks OslArchTransferToKernel and then ExAllocatePool in the kernel. A driver then watches for svchost processes running with the netsvcs argument and injects a user-mode stager via APC to reach a command-and-control server. The second-stage payload was not recovered.

Attribution rests on shared infrastructure: a Scrambled Cross implant reached command servers that resolved to the same IPs as the MoonBounce domain, and some used a certificate tied to APT41. Compilation timestamps and other backdoors on the network suggest long-term remote access. The closing advice covers firmware updates, TPM and Boot Guard where supported, firmware scanning, and training analysts to act on firmware alerts.

talks.title: CPU Fuzzing for Discovering Hardware caused Information Leakage Michael
talks.teaser: Shows how CPU fuzzing finds new microarchitectural side channels and attacks that leak data across cores and virtual machines.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how microarchitectural side channels and transient execution attacks can be found automatically rather than through slow manual analysis. Because this research depends on expertise and luck, the speaker applies fuzzing, a software testing technique, to CPUs. Each test uses a reset sequence, a trigger sequence and a measurement sequence of instructions, and compares cold and hot paths to reveal timing differences. This model rediscovers flush and reload on its own.

Running the approach on five AMD and Intel CPUs for about four days each rediscovered two known side channels and uncovered four new ones. Two attacks were built on them. One abuses the RDRAND instruction, whose latency rises across cores and virtual machines, enabling a covert channel between AWS instances without memory sharing or networking. Another shows that the non-temporal MOV can replace CLFLUSH, leaking more bytes per Meltdown access and breaking KASLR. A mutation-based fuzzer for data sampling attacks then ran for 26 hours, finding a new zombie load variant, Medusa, that leaked an OpenSSL RSA key, and a regression on Ice Lake.

The speaker concludes that these fuzzers are still simple and lack guidance, so progress needs feedback from performance counters, debug interfaces or other side channels. The tools and accompanying papers are open source on GitHub.

talks.title: NL 2021: Blackboxing Diebold-Nixdorf ATMs by Vladimir Kononovich
talks.teaser: Explains how researchers decrypted, re-signed and uploaded custom firmware to an ATM cash dispenser over USB.
talks.summary:
The talk covers research into a cash dispenser module from a well-known ATM vendor, started after the speaker's team obtained a pair of firmware files from a bank project. The files were encrypted. The speaker explains that the decryption routine is a modified XTEA cipher with a non-standard delta constant, and that its key material is read from a dedicated region of the controller board. The firmware header also checks for a special block that can point to alternate key offsets, which made it possible to work with keys the team did not hold.

The firmware signature was self-signed, so the team could re-sign modified images with a shorter RSA key, since the signature field size is set by the format. The modified image was then uploaded to the dispenser over USB, using the device identifiers to trigger the upgrade path. The smart card that protects USB traffic also had a denial-of-service issue. Requesting a session key for the maximum counter value blocked further key generation, although the speaker notes that reinitializing the applet restores it when vendor keys are available.

To complete the attack, the team patched the firmware so it no longer requested session keys from the smart card, adjusted the vendor Java software, and synchronized session counters. They then configured cassette contents, ran a cash-out, and opened the shutter to collect the banknotes. The speaker presents this as a black-box method that needs only a USB connection inside the dispenser and leaves no logs. The practical lesson is that self-signed firmware and weak key handling undermine otherwise strong transport protection. At the time of the talk, the related CVEs were still in the registration and confirmation process.

talks.title: How to perform electromagnetic side channel analysis by simulation by Davide | hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows how simulated electromagnetic traces of a chip can reveal leakage hotspots before the silicon is fabricated.
talks.summary:
Electromagnetic side-channel attacks need only one leaky position over a chip's surface to compromise a device, yet existing power analysis tools cannot show where that position is or how the physical layout affects it. The talk presents a simulation flow that models the magnetic field of a whole chip. Current flowing in the upper metal layers is extracted with a commercial tool, the Biot-Savart law turns each current segment into a magnetic field, and the flux through a probe's surface is differentiated over time to produce the voltage an oscilloscope would record.

Simulated traces are noise-free, so a standard correlation attack lights up almost the entire die, unlike measured maps. To address this, the speaker computes how much noise would have to be added to a simulated trace to push a correlation below significance, and reports a correlation only when the correct key guess stands out from the others. Validation on a test chip compared simulated and measured correlation maps across different probe heights and diameters, vertical and horizontal probes, and front-side versus back-side analysis, finding close agreement in the leaking areas and their intensities.

The flow was then applied at the design stage to locate leaky standard cells and to compare two chip variants with different power routing. The variant whose supply and ground rails carry current in opposing directions showed fewer and weaker leaking areas, matching the measurements. The speaker noted that simulation time did not visibly grow with circuit complexity. The takeaway for designers is that such a flow can assess electromagnetic robustness and guide layout changes before fabrication.

talks.title: NL 2021: Automated Vulnerability Hunting In SMM Using Brick by Assaf & Itai
talks.teaser: Shows how SMM handlers in UEFI firmware can be checked for memory corruption bugs using an automated IDA-based tool.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces System Management Mode, the highly privileged x86 CPU mode that firmware uses for tasks such as power management and legacy device emulation. It explains how SMM memory (SMRAM) is isolated from the operating system, and how software triggers system management interrupts through a communication buffer that lives outside protected memory. That buffer is the attack surface the rest of the talk focuses on.

The speaker then covers common bug classes in SMM handlers. A missing size check on the communication buffer can let writes spill into SMRAM. Unvalidated nested pointers can give an attacker an arbitrary write target. Double fetches of a value can be exploited by a DMA device that changes the buffer between the validation check and its later use. Each class is illustrated with a small example and its mitigation, such as explicit size checks and copying sensitive fields into SMRAM local variables.

The talk then presents Brick, an open-source static analysis tool built on IDA. It extracts SMM images from firmware, runs heuristic detection modules for each bug class, and writes an HTML report. A live demo scans several modules and highlights suspicious handlers, while code from the EDK2 reference implementation comes out clean. The speaker reports a few CVEs found with the tool, notes that the heuristics produce false positives and negatives so human review remains necessary, and invites contributions to improve detection accuracy and speed.

talks.title: Breaking chips with undetectable hardware trojans | Matt Venn | hardwear.io webinars 2021
talks.teaser: Shows how a change to a chip's doping layers can add a hidden trojan that alters logic without visible changes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short primer on how transistors work and how they combine into logic cells, using an inverter from the open SkyWater 130 nanometre design kit as the example. The speaker explains that layout files can be turned back into a netlist and simulated, even without the original design files, and demonstrates this on that small inverter.

The main demonstration uses a simple padlock chip built with the open-source OpenLane flow. The extracted circuit opens only with the correct button combination. The speaker then shows how changing just the diffusion layers, swapping the doping type in one transistor and cutting a connection in another, can force a flip-flop output high. Editing the layout in KLayout creates the altered mask data, and the simulation shows the lock opening on a wrong combination, one clock cycle sooner.

The talk closes on the limits of the attack. Inserting such a change requires access to the foundry's files, and mask sets are expensive, so the modification is framed as a proof of concept. Recovering the logic from a raw die is much harder without the process design kit. A large customer could counter it by requesting masks back for inspection, while shared shuttle runs make that impractical. The practical takeaway is that layout-level edits can change behaviour while looking identical under a microscope.

talks.title: Securing Your Microcontroller with Arm TrustZone Technology | Oren Hollander | hardwear_io Webinar
talks.teaser: Explains how Arm TrustZone for ARMv8-M isolates secure and non-secure code on microcontrollers.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why embedded software needs stronger isolation. The speaker walks through three real attacks: Stuxnet, which spread through Windows workstations and reached PLCs at an Iranian nuclear plant; LoJax, a UEFI firmware rootkit that survives operating system reinstalls; and a dynamic voltage and frequency scaling attack that can leak cryptographic keys from the secure area on Arm CPUs.

The core of the talk covers Arm TrustZone for ARMv8-M, the security extension aimed at Cortex-M microcontrollers. It explains how the address space is split into secure and non-secure regions using a Security Attribution Unit and an optional implementation-defined attribution unit, and how the two combine so that the stricter setting wins. It describes secure gateway veneers as the only controlled entry points from non-secure to secure code, how interrupts can be assigned to either world, and how registers are stacked and cleared on world switches. Toolchain support is covered too, including the CMSE extensions in GCC and Arm Compiler and SAU setup through CMSIS.

The closing section weighs what TrustZone does and does not stop. It protects software against software attacks, as long as the secure code itself has no bugs, and can block bus masters such as DMA when the silicon vendor uses the extra security signal. It does not stop glitching or power side-channel attacks, which need hardware countermeasures. Debug access to the secure world is governed by vendor-specific secure debug authentication, so practitioners should check what their chip provides.

talks.title: PCIe device security-The evolution of DMA attacks | Maggie & Cuauhtemoc | hardwear.io webinars 2021
talks.teaser: Traces the history of PCIe direct memory access attacks and the Intel features, like VT-d and SR-IOV, that defend against them.
talks.summary:
PCIe is a long-lived interconnect used in everything from small IoT boards to data center servers. The talk focuses on direct memory access (DMA), which lets a device read and write system memory without the CPU's involvement. That efficiency is also what makes it an attack path. The speakers argue that limiting physical access to expansion slots does not remove the risk, because integrated DMA engines and add-in cards with their own firmware can start memory transactions without the host's knowledge.

The presenters survey roughly two decades of DMA research and tooling, from early Windows kernel subversion and Thunderbolt work to FPGA-based implants and wireless DMA devices. They then cover defenses. Intel VT-d remaps device memory access so a device can only reach regions explicitly mapped to it, while SR-IOV splits one physical device into virtual functions that can be assigned to separate guests. For each, they outline benefits and tradeoffs, including the need to define DMAR tables correctly and the fact that VT-d does not isolate devices sharing an external PCIe bridge.

The closing section looks at emerging standards, including SPDM for device attestation and CXL for cache-coherent and memory-semantic links. The practical takeaways are to keep VT-d enabled for both pre-boot and runtime, review DMAR tables, keep devices behind the same bridge at the same trust level, and keep firmware and drivers current. A short Q&A covered how virtual functions are assigned and whether DMA can be used to capture memory for forensics.
